newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German tax cuts won't jeopardise EMU-Waigel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German tax cuts won't jeopardise EMU-Waigel.

text.p: Germany's coalition government on Thursday ended months of feuding by announcing tax cuts for 1998 and affirming that public borrowing would continue to meet targets required under Europe's single currency.

Leaders from the three-party alliance agreed to reduce the solidarity surcharge -- raised to channel aid to east Germany -- by two points to 5.5 percent, and cut corporate taxes, both from the start of 1998.
"This is a decision by the coalition for growth, jobs and investment, and it relieves the burden on taxpayers," Finance Minister Theo Waigel told a news conference.
The tax cuts mark the first phase of a major tax reform to take effect in 1999. But the overall package, with big income tax cuts, will only be completed in late January, he said.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) finalised a position paper on Wednesday after wrangling on taxes had come close to tearing apart his 14-year administration over the autumn.

The solidarity tax cut will chop 7.5 billion marks ($4.8 billion) from the country's tax bill, or 200 marks for an average wage-earner. But the corporate tax cuts will be offset by scrapping tax breaks.

Despite the reductions, Waigel said Germany would trim government borrowing further. He reaffirmed next year's budget deficit target of 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, and said that in 1998 that ratio would be lower.
Referring to the Maastricht treaty's deficit ceiling of three percent, Waigel said: "There are no disagreements that the three percent goal should be met in 1998, '99 and after."

Waigel also reaffirmed his forecast of 2.5 percent growth next year -- more optimistic than the latest projection by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) of 2.2 percent growth after 1.1 percent this year.

Waigel's negotiating partners Hermann Otto Solms (FDP) and Wolfgang Schaeuble (CDU) both declared themselves satisfied with the coalition paper, which would boost growth and give fresh hope to Germany's four million jobless.
Opposition leaders, however, branded the tax cuts as an attack on an eastern Germany still recovering economically from four decades of communist mismanagement.
"This is a decision against eastern Germany -- against the interests of our country and its unity," Greens parliamentary leader Joschka Fischer said in a statement.

In the paper, the three parties also said they would seek European Union approval to impose a value-added tax on energy consumption to help balance out the relationship between direct and indirect taxation in Germany.
Although keen to present a show of unity as they go for their Christmas break, the coalition leaders were tight-lipped about work on the main tax reform in 1999.

Waigel said plans would be completed by January 22 after three further meetings of a coalition working group. Already settled is that tax breaks of between 40 and 50 billion marks will be scrapped to help pay for tax cuts. ($1=1.5554 Mark)
